claim: Methylation of adenosines at the N6 position (m6A) is a dynamic and abundant epitranscriptomic mark that regulates critical aspects of eukaryotic RNA metabolism in numerous biological processes.

claim: Substitutions of Asp395METTL3 or Asn549/Gln550METTL3 to alanine reduced the methyltransferase activity of the complex to background levels.
source: Substitutions of Asp395METTL3 or Asn549/Gln550METTL3 to alanine reduced the methyltransferase activity of the complex to background levels (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Alanine substitutions of Glu192METTL14 or Pro362/Thr363METTL14 targeting the putative active site in METTL14 had little effect on the MTase activity of the METTL3-14 complex.
source: In contrast, alanine substitutions of Glu192METTL14 or Pro362/Thr363METTL14 targeting the putative active site in METTL14 had little effect on the MTase activity of the METTL3-14 complex (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The catalytic activity of the complex is restricted to the METTL3 active site.
source: These results indicate that the catalytic activity of the complex is restricted to the METTL3 active site
evidence: This is an inference from the mutagenesis data.

claim: METTL14 likely plays a non-catalytic role within the m6A writer complex.
source: and suggest that METTL14 likely plays a non-catalytic role within the m6A writer complex.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural and mutagenesis data.

claim: With the acceptor adenine bound in the active site of METTL3, the ribose-phosphate backbone of the RNA substrate is placed over a positively charged groove located at the interface of the METTL3 and METTL14 subunits.
source: With the acceptor adenine bound in the active site of METTL3, the ribose-phosphate backbone of the RNA substrate is placed over a positively charged groove located at the interface of the METTL3 and METTL14 subunits (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This claim is based on structural modeling shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: The positively charged groove is highly evolutionarily conserved and comprises residues Arg465METTL3, Arg468METTL3, His474METTL3, His478METTL3 and Arg245METTL14, Arg249METTL14, Arg254METTL14 and Arg255METTL14.
source: This groove is highly evolutionarily conserved and comprises residues Arg465METTL3, Arg468METTL3, His474METTL3, His478METTL3 and Arg245METTL14, Arg249METTL14, Arg254METTL14 and Arg255METTL14.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence conservation analysis.

claim: Residues Arg245METTL14, Arg249METTL14, Arg254METTL14 and Arg255METTL14 form a positively charged pocket occupied by a co-crystallized acetate ion, possibly mimicking RNA phosphate group binding.
source: The last four residues form a positively charged pocket occupied by a co-crystallized acetate ion, possibly mimicking RNA phosphate group binding (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The positively charged surface adjacent to the METTL3 active site mediates substrate RNA binding.
source: These observations suggest that this surface mediates substrate RNA binding
evidence: This is an inference from structural analysis.

claim: The surface adjacent to the putative active site in METTL14 on the opposite face of the METTL3-14 dimer lacks evolutionary conservation and is mostly negatively charged.
source: In contrast, the corresponding surface adjacent to the putative active site in METTL14 on the opposite face of the METTL3-14 dimer lacks evolutionary conservation and is mostly negatively charged (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural and conservation analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The activity of the R254AMETTL14 mutant complex was substantially lower than in the wild type.
source: The activity of the R254AMETTL14 mutant complex was substantially lower than in the wild type (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The catalytic activity of the R254A/R255AMETTL14 double mutant complex was reduced to background levels.
source: When Arg255METTL14 was additionally mutated to alanine, the catalytic activity of resulting R254A/R255AMETTL14 double mutant complex was reduced to background levels
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Arg254METTL14 and Arg255METTL14 are involved in substrate RNA binding.
source: further suggesting that these residues are involved in substrate RNA binding (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is an inference from the mutagenesis data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Alanine substitution of Tyr406METTL3 reduced the MTase activity of the complex to background level.
source: Alanine substitution of Tyr406METTL3 reduced the MTase activity of the complex to background level.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Substitution of Tyr198METTL14 had little effect on MTase activity.
source: In contrast, substitution of Tyr198METTL14 had little effect on MTase activity (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The m6A writer complex contains only one active site – in METTL3.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that the m6A writer complex contains only one active site – in METTL3
evidence: This is an inference from the structural and mutagenesis data.

claim: Substrate RNA binding is mediated by a conserved electropositive surface at the interface of the METTL3-14 subunits.
source: and that substrate RNA binding is mediated by a conserved electropositive surface at the interface of the METTL3-14 subunits.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural and mutagenesis data.

claim: The molecular architecture of the METTL3-METTL14 dimer is strikingly similar to that of homodimeric bacterial N6-adenosine DNA methyltransferases such as EcoP15I.
source: The molecular architecture of the METTL3-METTL14 dimer is strikingly similar to that of homodimeric bacterial N6-adenosine DNA methyltransferases such as EcoP15I.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison.

claim: The m6A writer enzyme may have emerged by the acquisition of a bacterial homodimeric DNA methyltransferase.
source: This hints at an evolutionary scenario in which the m6A writer enzyme emerged by the acquisition of a bacterial homodimeric DNA methyltransferase.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural similarity.

claim: Subsequent gene duplication and sequence divergence of the METTL3 and METTL14 subunits may have driven the specificity switch towards RNA.
source: Subsequent gene duplication and sequence divergence of the METTL3 and METTL14 subunits may have driven the specificity switch towards RNA.
evidence: This is a speculation about evolutionary history.

claim: The two methyltransferase subunits form an obligate, constitutive heterodimer.
source: The presence of an extensive interaction interface between METTL3 and METTL14 in the complex suggests that the two methyltransferase subunits form an obligate, constitutive heterodimer
evidence: This is an inference from the structural data.

claim: METTL3 and METTL14 are unlikely to be functional in isolation.
source: implying that they are unlikely to be functional in isolation.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural data.

claim: Soluble METTL14 could not be expressed in the absence of METTL3.
source: Of note, we have not been able to express and purify soluble METTL14 in the absence of METTL3
evidence: This is a direct observation from expression experiments.

claim: METTL3 is required to stabilize METTL14.
source: suggesting that METTL3 is required to stabilize METTL14.
evidence: This is an inference from the expression data.

claim: Knockout of either METTL3 or METTL14 in mouse embryonic stem cells resulted in complete loss of m6A modification in mRNA.
source: Our observations are fully consistent with a recent genetic study showing that knockout of either METTL3 or METTL14 in mouse embryonic stem cells resulted in complete loss of m6A modification in mRNA (Geula et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research (Geula et al., 2015).

claim: METTL14 has a twofold function in maintaining the integrity of the complex and in facilitating RNA substrate binding.
source: These observations suggest that METTL14 is not catalytically active and likely has a twofold function in maintaining the integrity of the complex and in facilitating RNA substrate binding
evidence: This is an inference from the structural and mutagenesis data.

claim: The N-terminal extension of METTL3 is required for the MTase activity of the core m6A complex.
source: However, given that the truncated complex used for crystallographic analysis lacks catalytic activity in vitro compared to the complexes containing full-length METTL3, the N-terminal extension of METTL3 is also required for the MTase activity of the core m6A complex.
evidence: This is an inference from the activity data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The two N-terminal CCCH zinc finger motifs of METTL3 may be essential for catalytic activity, perhaps by contributing to specific recognition of the consensus methylation sequence.
source: It is tempting to speculate that the two N-terminal CCCH zinc finger motifs of METTL3 are essential for catalytic activity, perhaps by contributing to specific recognition of the consensus methylation sequence.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural and activity data.

claim: Additional sequences in the N-terminal low complexity region of METTL14 are dispensable for catalytic activity.
source: Interestingly, despite the spatial proximity of the N-terminal extension of METTL14 to the active site of METTL3 (Figure 2A), additional sequences in the N-terminal low complexity region of METTL14 are dispensable for catalytic activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.
